title: Why Did Christianity Grow Differently in South Korea and Japan?
author: Natural experiment
focus: Two wealthy East Asian allies look surprisingly alike, until the religion numbers split wide open.
framing: Two nearby countries share a modern neighborhood, high development, deep ties to the United States, and long histories shaped by Buddhism and Confucian learning. So why did Christianity become much more common in South Korea than in Japan?

comparisonPoints.label: Modern development
comparisonPoints.detail: World Bank data puts Japan and South Korea close in 2025 GDP per person, at about $35,951 and $36,227.

comparisonPoints.label: Everyday modern life
comparisonPoints.detail: The World Bank reports similar life expectancy in 2024: about 84.0 years in Japan and 83.6 years in South Korea.

comparisonPoints.label: Postwar alliances
comparisonPoints.detail: The U.S. State Department describes both relationships as enduring security alliances.

reveal.label: The surprise
reveal.detail: Pew Research Center's 2023 East Asia survey found 32% of South Korean adults identify as Christian, compared with 2% in Japan.

scriptParagraphs: Here is the mystery. Japan and South Korea are neighbors. Both are wealthy, high-tech democracies. Both became close allies of the United States after devastating wars.

According to the World Bank, their 2025 GDP per person was almost side by side: about thirty-five thousand nine hundred dollars in Japan and thirty-six thousand two hundred dollars in South Korea. Their life expectancy is close too.
So we have to ask the learning question: are these two countries comparable enough that a big difference should make us curious?

Pew Research Center found that in a 2023 survey, thirty-two percent of South Korean adults identified as Christian. In Japan, it was two percent. That is about one out of three adults in South Korea, compared with about one out of fifty in Japan.

The easy guesses do not quite work. It is not just America, because America was deeply connected to both countries. It is not just wealth and technology, because both countries are highly developed. It is not simply East Asia resisting Christianity, because South Korea does not fit that story.
So we look for what Christianity seemed to be attached to in each place.

In Japan, Christianity arrived early and grew for a while. Then the Tokugawa shogunate, the warrior government that ruled Japan for more than two hundred years, treated it as dangerous. Christianity was banned. Christians had to hide. Imagine if joining a church made your family look like it was helping a foreign enemy.

In Korea, Protestant missionaries later became connected not only with preaching, but also with schools, hospitals, reading, women's education, and modern medicine. And when Korea was ruled by Japan, some Christian institutions could feel like places to learn, organize, and keep a little room to breathe.
So the difference is not that one people was naturally this way and another people was naturally that way. It is about what the same religion came wearing.
In one place: danger sign. In another place: schoolbag, hospital bag, and sometimes a flag of resistance.
The final question is: when a new idea arrives somewhere, what does it look like to the people opening the door?

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Japan and South Korea are neighbors. Both are wealthy, high-tech democracies. Both became close allies of the United States after devastating wars.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: So this is a proper comparison, not just two random countries tossed into the same basket.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [prim, checking] So this is a proper comparison, not just two random countries tossed into the same basket.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Yes, Audrey. First we ask: are they comparable enough that a big difference should make us curious?

dialogueSegments.text: According to the World Bank, their 2025 GDP per person was almost side by side: about thirty-five thousand nine hundred dollars in Japan and thirty-six thousand two hundred dollars in South Korea.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: That is closer than I would have guessed.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [softly, surprised] That is closer than I would have guessed.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Their life expectancy is close too: about eighty-four years in Japan and eighty-three point six in South Korea.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: Neighbors. Wealthy. Technological. Long lives. Allied with the United States. I am arranging the evidence in a neat pile.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [precise] Neighbors. Wealthy. Technological. Long lives. Allied with the United States. I am arranging the evidence in a neat pile.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Good. Now the reveal.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Pew Research Center found that in a 2023 survey, thirty-two percent of South Korean adults identified as Christian. In Japan, it was two percent.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Does that difference sound significant?

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: Significant? It is practically waving a little flag and shouting, investigate me.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [incredulous] Significant? It is practically waving a little flag and shouting, investigate me.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: It means about one out of three adults in South Korea, compared with about one out of fifty in Japan.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: One out of three. And one out of fifty. How uncanny.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [wondering] One out of three. And one out of fifty. How uncanny.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Pause there.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Hmm. Interesting.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Now we test some guesses.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: I shall begin with the obvious suspect: America.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [decisive] I shall begin with the obvious suspect: America.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Fair. But America was deeply connected to both countries after the Second World War. So America alone cannot explain why one number is thirty-two and the other is two.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: So that door opens a little, but not all the way.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [softly] So that door opens a little, but not all the way.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Exactly. Second guess: maybe rich, high-tech countries all become less religious in the same way.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: But these two rich, high-tech countries ended up with very different Christian populations.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: So money and phones do not solve the mystery. Noted.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [crisp] So money and phones do not solve the mystery. Noted.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Third guess: maybe East Asia simply leaves very little room for Christianity.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: But South Korea proves that answer is too easy.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: Then it is not just where the idea arrives. It is what happens to it after it arrives.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [thoughtful] Then it is not just where the idea arrives. It is what happens to it after it arrives.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Beautifully put, Paxten.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: So now we look at what Christianity seemed to be wearing in each place.

dialogueSegments.text: In Japan, Christianity arrived early and grew for a while. Then the Tokugawa shogunate treated it as dangerous.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: I've heard of the Tokugawa. A shogunate was like a military government run by samurai warriors, yes?
dialogueSegments.audioText: [eager, precise] I've heard of the Tokugawa. A shogunate was like a military government run by samurai warriors, yes?

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Yes, Audrey. A shogun was the top military ruler. The Tokugawa family ruled Japan for more than two hundred years.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: So not a small club with matching hats. A whole government.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [primly] So not a small club with matching hats. A whole government.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: A whole government. And that government banned Christianity. Christians had to hide.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Imagine if joining a church made your family look like it was helping a foreign enemy.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: That would make the word Christian feel frightening before anyone even explained it.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [quietly] That would make the word Christian feel frightening before anyone even explained it.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Yes. The idea did not just arrive as a religion. To Japan's rulers, it could look like a danger sign.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: Do you mean to say that the same idea can arrive wearing a different costume?
dialogueSegments.audioText: [brightening] Do you mean to say that the same idea can arrive wearing a different costume?

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Exactly. Now compare Korea.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: In Korea, Protestant missionaries later became connected not only with preaching, but also with schools, hospitals, reading, women's education, and modern medicine.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: So Christianity could arrive with a schoolbag and a doctor's bag.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [gently] So Christianity could arrive with a schoolbag and a doctor's bag.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Yes. And when Korea was ruled by Japan, some Christian institutions could feel like places to learn, organize, and keep a little room to breathe.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: So in Japan, danger sign. In Korea, schoolbag, hospital bag, and sometimes a flag of resistance.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [with precision and excitement] So in Japan, danger sign. In Korea, schoolbag, hospital bag, and sometimes a flag of resistance.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: You would not expect the same religion to feel so different.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [soft wonder] You would not expect the same religion to feel so different.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: That is the natural experiment.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: The answer is not that one country is naturally Christian and the other naturally not. It is about timing, fear, trust, schools, hospitals, colonial rule, and what people thought Christianity was attached to.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Paxten
dialogueSegments.text: Let me consider that a bit.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [softly] Let me consider that a bit.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: Please do.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Audrey
dialogueSegments.text: I think I have it. When a new idea arrives, we should ask what people think it is carrying.
dialogueSegments.audioText: [satisfied] I think I have it. When a new idea arrives, we should ask what people think it is carrying.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: That is the question to keep.

dialogueSegments.speaker: Narrator
dialogueSegments.text: When a new idea knocks on the door, does it look like a threat, a tool, a school, a hospital, a protest, or a promise?
